rules.title: A startup entry that runs something out of a temporary folder
rules.why: A temporary folder is emptied by the system and by cleaners, so an entry there is one that expects to be re-created rather than installed.
rules.benign: An installer that registers a temporary shim and removes it when it finishes.
rules.remediation: Quarantine the binary, then remove the startup entry.

rules.title: An unsigned startup entry in the user's own scope
rules.why: A signature is a fact about the file, not a verdict: unsigned means the author did not buy a certificate, and nothing more.
rules.benign: A small open-source launcher, or a self-built binary, that has never been signed.
rules.remediation: Open the folder and look at the file before removing anything. The hash is in the finding.

rules.title: A process running from a temporary folder
rules.why: Programs are installed, not left in the folder the system empties; a process there is either passing through or hiding in it.
rules.benign: A portable application that unpacks itself and runs from its own extraction folder.
rules.remediation: Look at the process's parent and command line before acting; the details are in the panel.

rules.title: A socket waiting for a connection on every interface
rules.why: A socket bound to every interface is reachable from the network, which is a decision someone made rather than a default most programs choose.
rules.benign: A development server or a file-sharing program the person started deliberately.
rules.remediation: Close the program, or bind it to loopback in its settings. The owning process is in the row.

rules.title: A service's DLL is in a folder a user can write
rules.why: A service runs as SYSTEM, and the code it loads is normally installed where only an administrator can write. A DLL under a folder the signed-in user can write starts SYSTEM-level code that a non-administrator can replace.
rules.benign: A per-user certificate store, a printer driver or a vendor's own service that installs into ProgramData and upgrades itself there.
rules.remediation: Open the folder and look at the DLL's publisher and its date. If nobody installed it deliberately, disable the service before touching the file.

rules.title: A netsh helper DLL is named by a full path in a user-writable folder
rules.why: Every netsh command loads its helpers into the netsh process, so a helper DLL is code that runs whenever anyone runs netsh. A helper named by a bare file name is resolved from the system folder; one named by a full path outside it can be replaced by whoever can write that path.
rules.benign: A vendor's own network tooling that installs a helper beside its application and registers it by full path.
rules.remediation: Look at the DLL's publisher and its date. If no network tool was installed deliberately, remove the value and the file.

rules.title: A print monitor DLL is named by a full path in a user-writable folder
rules.why: The print spooler runs as SYSTEM and loads monitor DLLs by name, so a monitor whose driver is a full path in a writable folder is code that runs with the spooler's rights.
rules.benign: A print vendor's port monitor installed with its driver package into ProgramData.
rules.remediation: Check the DLL's publisher. Remove the monitor's key only after stopping the spooler, or uninstall the print software that installed it.

rules.title: A time provider DLL is in a user-writable folder
rules.why: The Windows time service loads provider DLLs, and it runs as SYSTEM. A provider outside the system folder is a DLL loaded by a privileged service on every time sync.
rules.benign: A virtualisation guest agent that ships its own time provider and installs it beside itself.
rules.remediation: Check whether a hypervisor guest agent installed it. If not, remove the provider key and the DLL.

rules.title: The screensaver runs a program from a user-writable folder
rules.why: A screensaver is a program Windows starts by itself when the session is idle, which makes the setting a way to run something without a person clicking anything.
rules.benign: A screensaver a person downloaded and installed themselves, which is how most screensavers arrive.
rules.remediation: If you did not choose this screensaver, clear the setting in Windows' lock-screen options and remove the file.

rules.title: A hidden scheduled task runs a program from a user-writable folder
rules.why: Task Scheduler's Hidden setting takes a task out of its own list while leaving it scheduled, so a hidden task in a writable folder is both a thing that runs on a trigger and a thing its owner does not see.
rules.benign: Some updaters register a hidden maintenance task in ProgramData, and say so in their documentation.
rules.remediation: Open Task Scheduler as an administrator, find the task by the name in the finding, and read its action before disabling it.

rules.title: An editor or agent configuration that names a command to run
rules.why: A configuration that runs a command is a startup path with a different name, and it is read by a program the person trusts.
rules.benign: A task or hook the person wrote themselves in their own editor.
rules.remediation: Read the configuration file the finding names, then remove the hook if you did not write it.
